picks.note: hook — yeast bubbling in action (take 4)
picks.text: This is yeast bubbling in action.

picks.note: hook — way too excited about yeast (take 3)
picks.text: This is me, way too excited about yeast.

picks.note: name + promise (take 5)
picks.text: Katie, I'm a food scientist, and this is my deep dive into yeast.

picks.note: as humans, thousands of years
picks.text: As humans, we started using yeast thousands of years ago.

picks.note: records are murky
picks.text: The records for when yeast first showed up is kind of murky from what I could find in my research.

picks.note: about 3,000 years ago / 1,000 BC
picks.text: about 3,000 years ago, about 1,000 BC.

picks.note: Egypt, buried with pharaohs
picks.text: we see some in Egypt buried with pharaohs.

picks.note: jars, yeast on the side, DNA
picks.text: They have jars, yeast on the side from what the DNA test can solve.

picks.note: Asia into Europe, no way to know which was first
picks.text: We also have yeast showing up in the archaeological records from Asia into Europe, all over the place. We don't have exact ways of knowing which one was first, where they were, if we got all of the records, but we know it's all over the place.

picks.note: DNA is mixed in with everything else
picks.text: It's hard to pull out the DNA because it's also mixed in with a bunch of other things from my understanding.

picks.note: passed brewer to baker, off grapes, in the air
picks.text: Then we have this understanding of yeast. It's being passed between brewers and bakers. It's being collected from the air. It's being collected from outside of grapes and introduced into wine. It's moving around. It's passed from person to person, baker to brewer, brewer to baker. It's in meat. It's in wine. It's in beer. It's in our sourdough starters. It's just all around.

picks.note: successful batch passed on, dud batch dropped
picks.text: what they're doing is they're passing it from successful batch passed on to someone else's and they make a successful batch and if it's a dud batch they don't pass it on because who wants to do anything with a dud batch

picks.note: that is selective breeding
picks.text: And so what we're getting is selective breeding of good yeast, yeast that ferments, that makes the bread bubble, makes the alcohol happen, is being passed around. And that is what we've used for years and years and years.

picks.note: spontaneous generation → Pasteur's gooseneck flask
picks.text: and it was just thought it was spontaneous generation that's what it was until we get to louis pasteur louis pasteur comes in and he does his gooseneck bottle experiment and proves that it's not spontaneous generation that is making food come alive it is bacteria it's fungi it's a bunch of microscopic little things in our food and that's it that's all we know for a while with about yeast

picks.note: Meyen, 1838 → Saccharomyces cerevisiae
picks.text: And then we get Franz Julius Ferdinand Mayen. in 1838. He comes in and he discovers what we know for most of our yeast today, Saccharomyces cerevisiae. And that is the yeast that we see in our active dry yeast. It's what we find in our fresh yeast, our instant yeast, and most of our sourdoughs.

picks.note: the jars: mead, instant, active dry, fresh, pre-ferment
picks.text: I have marketing for yeast for mead. It's Saccharomyces cerevisiae. I have instant dry yeast. It's Saccharomyces cerevisiae. I have active dry yeast with a little sugar in it. Guess what? Saccharomyces cerevisiae. Fresh yeast. Saccharomyces cerevisiae. I even have what could be the start of a sourdough starter. Here, it's a pre-ferment. It is yeast, Saccharomyces cerevisiae mixed with flour and water.

picks.note: ~90% of the yeast we use is this one bug
picks.text: It is like 90% of all the yeast that we use is this one bug.

picks.note: sourdough changes batch to batch, mother to mother
picks.text: And in sourdoughs, we have, it's in most of the sourdoughs, but sourdough is where we see it change from batch to batch, mother to mother.

picks.note: other yeasts + bacteria are what make sourdough different
picks.text: there might be some other yeast inside of those batches and they have other bacteria and that's what makes sourdough just a little bit different than your everyday yeast, flour, pre-ferment like I have here.

picks.note: what yeast is — fungus, single cell, eukaryotic
picks.text: Okay, so what is yeast in and of itself? Yeast in and of itself is a, it's a small little bug, it's a fungi, it's single cell organism, it's eukaryotic,

picks.note: budding — mother, daughter, mitosis
picks.text: It reproduces itself by budding where a mother... cell will start to grow a little bud off of it for a daughter cell and the daughter cell once it gets big enough mitosis happens and it splits and then it and then it continues to grow and those split and those split

picks.note: same guy, home bakery to the vineyards
picks.text: and that is how Saccharomyces cerevisiae splits and grows and reproduces all over we use it everywhere from our home bakeries to the brewers down the road to the vineyards in California and France, everywhere, Saccharomyces cerevisiae, same guy, again and again and again.

picks.note: it thrives where it is fed — starches and sugars
picks.text: So it will bud and reproduce in an environment that it thrives in. It likes it to be nutritionally dense for it. That's where it likes having starches and sugars to break down and give the energy that it needs to continue to grow.

picks.note: 54 °F to just over 100 °F
picks.text: It likes its temperature between 54 degrees Fahrenheit and just over 100 degrees Fahrenheit.

picks.note: underneath 54 degrees —
picks.text: Underneath 54 degrees,

picks.note: — it hibernates until it warms back up
picks.text: it goes back into a little shell of itself and hibernates and it just tucks away and takes a nap until it warms back up and is a good environment for it to grow and thrive and that's how it survives not being able to move from environment to environment.

picks.note: over 100 °F, and 140 °F kills it
picks.text: Over 100 degrees it can still grow until it gets to about 140 degrees Fahrenheit and that's when baking happens and it kills it off in the oven

picks.note: oven spring, and no live yeast in baked bread
picks.text: You might get oven spring from the yeast still growing and other things happening but then it stops and you're not eating fresh yeast when you eat bread because you've killed it off.

picks.note: CHEMISTRY — starch → amylase → sucrose → invertase
picks.text: Okay, so you have your starch and it breaks down with alpha amylase and beta amylase. And we'll get into that in another video. And then that breaks down to sucrose. And sucrose... exists around the yeast and the yeast itself provides invertase. And invertase is an enzyme. If it ends in "-ase", it's an enzyme. And so the invertase goes in to sucrose and breaks it down into glucose and fructose.

picks.note: CHEMISTRY — zymase → CO₂ + alcohol
picks.text: You get zymase and it breaks it down into your CO2 and your alcohol. That's your carbon dioxide and your alcohol.

picks.note: both burn off when you bake it
picks.text: And then when you bake the bread, the alcohol and the CO2 kind of burn off and leave the bread. So they're not behind left in the bread after you've cooked it.

picks.note: the CO₂ is why champagne is bubbly
picks.text: And you also have your CO2. That's where you get your bubbly wines like your champagne.

picks.note: fat, salt and spice in the dough —
picks.text: In your dough, you have fats, salts, spices.

picks.note: — get between the yeast and its food
picks.text: in the way between the yeast and the sugar and the starches that it wants to eat. And so it slows it down. It takes longer. It's harder for the yeast to reach its food source. It can get there. It just takes more time.

picks.note: so factor in more proofing time
picks.text: So when you're cooking with added fat, salt, spices to a a dough you just need to factor in that it's going to take more time for it to proof for it to get to what it needs because it needs starches sugars it needs water that's all it needs

picks.note: a pre-ferment is flour, water, yeast
picks.text: A pre-ferment is flour, water, yeast. That's all is needed.

picks.note: you do not need sugar to activate it
picks.text: I know some yeast says it needs sugar to activate active dry yeast. They recommend that. Really, if you give it time, you don't need the sugar in it. You don't have to add the sugar to your dough unless that is a, you want a sweeter dough.

picks.note: sugar buys speed and costs you a sweeter bread
picks.text: So it just, how much time do you want? If you need to bake dough and you want it to rise a little bit faster, you can add sugar to it. It's just going to be a sweeter bread, but it will rise a little faster, get going a little faster, shorten your proofing time.

picks.note: if it is all one organism, why so many products?
picks.text: Saccharomyces cerevisiae, I said it's all the same thing, but why? Why do we have so many different forms when it's all the same guy? Well, he likes to go dormant. He might die.

picks.note: it needs access to food
picks.text: He needs access to food sources.

picks.note: it comes down to how often you need it
picks.text: it comes down to how frequently does the person using it need to have access to the yeast.

picks.note: a working baker uses it daily → fresh yeast
picks.text: A baker is using yeast day in and day out. They can have fresh yeast on hand because they might not want to wait for a dry yeast to come building back up into active yeast that is moving and flowing. Having fresh yeast will shorten their cook time, their baking time, their proof time, and it makes it easier.

picks.note: an hour from a grocery store → active dry / instant
picks.text: If you have a baker in Kansas that lives on a farm that takes an hour to get to their local grocery store, having fresh yeast... is not practical because they need something that can stay on hand, that lasts longer. That's where you get your active dry and your instant yeast needs. It's a casual baker, a person that doesn't want something that is gonna go and die within a couple weeks, a week. They need something that lasts longer because of the effort it takes to get to the grocery store.

picks.note: and those shops —
picks.text: Also, those grocery stores

picks.note: — probably do not sell much yeast
picks.text: probably don't sell a lot of yeast because they might not have as frequent customers.

picks.note: stock that dies on the shelf is not viable
picks.text: And so having fresh yeast on hand and having it die on hand again and again might not be financially viable. So they have the dry yeast on hand so that way when the customer comes in, it's available, it's not dead, it's... It's what those people need.

picks.note: brewer's yeast — marketing, convenience, the customer
picks.text: But if you have yeast on hand and you have someone that's wanting to learn how to brew, they're searching, how do I find yeast? And they get brewer's yeast. Yes, I'm brewing. Let me buy brewer's yeast. It's marketing sometimes. Sometimes it's convenience. Sometimes it's who the customer is. But if you know what you're looking for, you can buy what you can find and work with it.

picks.note: if you want the best loaf, instant vs active dry differs
picks.text: If you're really wanting to deep dive into making the best, most perfect bread, the most premium bread, you might care what type of yeast, because there is a little bit of a difference with instant and active dry.

picks.note: CHEMISTRY — drying damages it; it releases glutathione
picks.text: And so the yeast might become damaged from sitting and being dried out and when it comes up and back to life, it can release something called glutathione.

picks.note: CHEMISTRY — glutathione attacks the gluten matrix
picks.text: And what that can do is it can get into the gluten matrix and attack it a little bit.

picks.note: so the bread is not as stretchy
picks.text: So you have your your instant dry yeast, what you might find is one of the, it's available, it's findable, but one of the offsets might be that the bread is not as stretchy.

picks.note: and it dries out faster
picks.text: The bread might dry out a little faster because the starch has a harder time holding onto water with the GSH involved.

picks.note: day to day, does it matter? probably not
picks.text: And so day to day, does it really matter? Probably not with the bread that you want to make.

picks.note: but if it does, try switching to fresh
picks.text: But if it really matters, if you're finding that your bread is drying out, it's not as stretchy, it's not as elastic as you want the bite to be, try seeing if you can find fresh yeast and switching to that. That might help fix the problem that you run into.

picks.note: otherwise use what you can get
picks.text: But if you're happy with your bread, it doesn't matter if you have access to fresh yeast. Active dry works great. If you have fresh yeast available but you can't find for some reason the active dry or instant yeast, go ahead and use that. Use what's available.

picks.note: it is all the same — look at sourdough
picks.text: It's all the same. It's what we've done for hundreds of years. I mean, look at our ancestors who made sourdough.

picks.note: sourdough was what was available out west
picks.text: Sourdough was what was available. They didn't have to ship back, ship yeast from back east to the hard to reach people. And so that's why some people, sourdough is even better than active dry yeast for them.

picks.note: you can start a sourdough from active dry
picks.text: And if you're struggling because you want a fresh yeast, and all you can find is active dry, try just making sourdough from your active dry. Get it going, get it started, let the yeast multiply, be happy for a few days, and then you have a little pre-ferment already made and go from there.

picks.note: close — it feels like a mystery, it is one bug
picks.text: It can be played with. Yeast is not something that has to be a hard and fast rule. It feels like a mystery, but really all it is is the same little Saccharomyces cerevisiae bug again and again and again and again. He's happy. All the little bug wants is to go and eat sugars and fart.

picks.note: close — CO₂ and ethanol, a happy life
picks.text: produce carbon dioxide and ethanol. It just wants to live a happy life and it's not all that complicated.
